WITH nights AS (                      -- one row per listing per listed night inside the window
  SELECT l.listing_id, l.city, g.night::date AS night
  FROM listings l
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(
         GREATEST(l.listed_from, DATE '{{start_date}}'),
         LEAST(COALESCE(l.listed_until, DATE '{{end_date}}'), DATE '{{end_date}}') - 1,
         interval '1 day') AS g(night)
), marked AS (
  SELECT n.city,
         date_trunc('month', n.night)::date AS month,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reservations r
                 WHERE r.listing_id = n.listing_id AND r.status = 'confirmed'
                   AND r.check_in <= n.night AND n.night < r.check_out) AS booked,
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM calendar_blocks b
                 WHERE b.listing_id = n.listing_id
                   AND b.start_date <= n.night AND n.night < b.end_date) AS blocked
  FROM nights n
)
SELECT city, month,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE booked)                AS booked_nights,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE booked OR NOT blocked) AS available_nights,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE booked)::numeric
             / COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE booked OR NOT blocked), 4) AS occupancy
FROM marked
GROUP BY city, month
HAVING COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE booked OR NOT blocked) > 0
ORDER BY city, month;

Explanation. The unit of occupancy is a listing-night, so the query builds exactly those: each listing's listed range clipped to the window, one row per night. Stays that cross a month boundary or the window's edges then need no special handling: each night lands in its own month, and nights outside the window were never generated. Two EXISTS checks mark each night: booked by a confirmed reservation (half-open), blocked by any block (also half-open, and EXISTS counts a night once however many blocks cover it). The denominator is booked OR NOT blocked, which is the Very Hard rule (a booked night is available whatever blocks cover it) and is harmless below it. Grouping the night grid, rather than joining reservations to a list of months, keeps city-months with no bookings.

Complexity. O(listing-nights × (reservations + blocks per listing)) as written; with an index on (listing_id, check_in) each EXISTS is a short range probe. The grid is the cost: a year of a large market is tens of millions of rows. An interval formulation (LEAST(check_out, month_end) − GREATEST(check_in, month_start) per stay and month, minus the blocked-and-not-booked nights computed from merged blocks) avoids expanding nights and is what follow-up 1 is after.

Snowflake: no generate_series; join to a calendar table or TABLE(GENERATOR(ROWCOUNT => n)) with DATEADD, COUNT_IF, DATE_TRUNC('month', night). Spark SQL: explode(sequence(start, end - 1, interval 1 day)), count_if. MySQL 8: a recursive CTE or a calendar table; SUM(CASE …).

WITH first_cancel AS (                -- the earliest cancellation event decides the notice
  SELECT booking_id, MIN(cancelled_at) AS cancelled_at
  FROM cancellations
  GROUP BY booking_id
), c AS (
  SELECT b.booking_id, b.policy, b.booked_at, b.check_in, b.nights,
         b.nightly_cents, b.cleaning_cents, b.service_fee_cents, f.cancelled_at,
         FLOOR(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM b.check_in - f.cancelled_at) / 86400)::int AS days_before,
         f.cancelled_at < b.check_in AS before_check_in
  FROM bookings b
  JOIN first_cancel f ON f.booking_id = b.booking_id
), tier AS (                          -- the most generous tier that applies
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (c.booking_id)
         c.booking_id, t.nightly_refund_pct, t.service_fee_refunded
  FROM c
  JOIN policy_tiers t ON t.policy = c.policy
  WHERE CASE WHEN c.before_check_in
             THEN c.days_before >= t.min_notice_days
                  AND (t.max_hours_after_booking IS NULL
                       OR c.cancelled_at <= c.booked_at + make_interval(hours => t.max_hours_after_booking))
             ELSE t.min_notice_days = 0 AND t.max_hours_after_booking IS NULL
        END
  ORDER BY c.booking_id, t.nightly_refund_pct DESC
)
SELECT c.booking_id, c.policy, c.days_before, t.nightly_refund_pct,
       ( (CASE WHEN c.before_check_in THEN c.nights
               ELSE GREATEST(c.nights - (FLOOR(EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM c.cancelled_at - c.check_in) / 86400)::int + 1), 0)
          END)::bigint * c.nightly_cents * t.nightly_refund_pct + 50 ) / 100
       + CASE WHEN c.before_check_in
              THEN c.cleaning_cents + CASE WHEN t.service_fee_refunded THEN c.service_fee_cents ELSE 0 END
              ELSE 0 END AS refund_cents
FROM c
JOIN tier t ON t.booking_id = c.booking_id
ORDER BY c.booking_id;

Explanation. One cancellation per booking first: the earliest cancelled_at, because a retried request logged later does not change when the guest cancelled (event ids are not time order). Notice is computed from the instants, floor(seconds / 86400), so "at least N days" is exactly days_before >= N, inclusive at the boundary second. The rules stay in the table: the booking joins every tier of its policy that applies and DISTINCT ON … ORDER BY pct DESC keeps the most generous; the grace tier simply has one more condition (cancelled_at <= booked_at + max_hours). Money is integer arithmetic: (cents × pct + 50) / 100 is half-up rounding for non-negative amounts. Very Hard: at or after check-in, nights whose start (check_in + k days) is at or before cancelled_at are spent; the rest are refunded at the base tier, without fees.

Complexity. One aggregate over cancellations, a join to a handful of tiers per booking and one sort: O(n log n). Tiny in practice; the value is in the rules being data.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: TIMESTAMP_DIFF(check_in, cancelled_at, SECOND) and DIV(…, 86400) (careful: DIV truncates toward zero, so use FLOOR(x / 86400) for negative notice), QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() … = 1, TIMESTAMP_ADD(booked_at, INTERVAL h HOUR). Snowflake: DATEDIFF('second', …), QUALIFY, DATEADD(hour, h, booked_at); DATEDIFF('day', …) counts calendar-day boundaries, not 24-hour periods, so it gives the wrong notice. Spark SQL: unix_timestamp differences, row_number() in a subquery. MySQL 8: TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, …), ROW_NUMBER() in a CTE, DIV for integer division.

Edge cases built into the data. Cancellations exactly N days before check-in and one second later, for two policies (every level); an odd nightly price at a 50% tier, so the refund has half a cent; bookings never cancelled. Hard: the strict grace tier exactly 48 hours after booking (applies), one second later (does not), and within 48 hours but too close to check-in; two cancellation events per booking, the later-logged one earlier in time. Very Hard: mid-stay cancellations, one exactly at check-in (night 1 begun), one exactly when night 3 begins, one after check-out (nothing left).

Common mistakes. Calendar-date differences (check_in::date - cancelled_at::date) instead of 24-hour periods; > at the boundary; the latest or the lowest-event_id cancellation; a hand-written CASE that ignores the tier table; ignoring max_hours_after_booking, or applying the grace tier on notice alone; dropping the cleaning fee or always refunding the service fee; floating-point percentages and ROUND on a float; mid-stay refunds counting the night that begins exactly at the cancellation as unspent.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The policy in force at booking time must be snapshotted on the booking (policy id and version), not joined from the listing's current setting. (2) The amount owed is fixed in the currency the guest paid, at booking; any later conversion is a payout concern recorded with its own rate. (3) A refunds ledger with one row per refund event (type: policy, partial, goodwill; amount; currency; reference to the booking) reconciled against an "owed" view like this one. (4) Effective-dated tiers (valid_from, valid_to) or a policy version id referenced from the booking; never edit a tier in place.

Rubric anchors. 2: right for simple cases but calendar-date notice, a hard-coded CASE or the wrong cancellation event. 3: matches the expected result. 4: also snapshots policies on bookings, fixes the currency of the obligation and versions the rules.

WITH scope AS (                       -- inquiries in the reporting window, with their host
  SELECT i.inquiry_id, i.listing_id, i.created_at, l.host_id
  FROM inquiries i
  JOIN listings l ON l.listing_id = i.listing_id
  WHERE i.created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_start}}'
    AND i.created_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '{{window_end}}'
), host_side AS (                     -- who may answer for a listing
  SELECT listing_id, host_id AS user_id FROM listings
  UNION
  SELECT listing_id, user_id FROM listing_cohosts
), first_reply AS (
  SELECT m.inquiry_id, MIN(m.sent_at) AS replied_at
  FROM messages m
  JOIN inquiries i ON i.inquiry_id = m.inquiry_id
  JOIN host_side h ON h.listing_id = i.listing_id AND h.user_id = m.sender_id
  WHERE NOT m.is_automated
  GROUP BY m.inquiry_id
), resp AS (
  SELECT s.host_id,
         EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM f.replied_at - s.created_at) / 60 AS minutes   -- NULL if unanswered
  FROM scope s
  LEFT JOIN first_reply f ON f.inquiry_id = s.inquiry_id
)
SELECT host_id,
       COUNT(*)                                   AS inquiries,
       COUNT(minutes)                             AS answered,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE minutes <= 1440)    AS within_24h,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE minutes <= 1440)::numeric / COUNT(*), 4) AS share_within_24h,
       ROUND((PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes))::numeric, 1) AS median_response_minutes
FROM resp
GROUP BY host_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= {{min_inquiries}}
ORDER BY host_id;

Explanation. The grain is the inquiry: each gets its host and the time of its first qualifying reply, or NULL. The qualifying filter (host side, not automated) is applied before MIN, so a guest's follow-up or an instant automated message can never be the "first reply". The LEFT JOIN keeps unanswered inquiries, which belong in inquiries and in the share's denominator but not in the median; COUNT(minutes) and PERCENTILE_CONT both skip NULLs, which is exactly that. PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) interpolates, so an even count gives the average of the two middle values. The window filters on created_at only; replies are searched without a time bound, so a late reply to an in-window inquiry still counts. At Medium the window spans every inquiry and the floor is 1; below Very Hard listing_cohosts is empty, so the host side is the host.

Complexity. One pass over messages with a hash join to the host side, one aggregate per inquiry and one per host: O(m + n log n) for the median's sort per host. At scale the per-inquiry first-reply table is the reusable intermediate.

Dialect notes (described, not executed). BigQuery: PERCENTILE_CONT(minutes, 0.5) OVER (PARTITION BY host_id) is analytic only, so take it in a subquery (or APPROX_QUANTILES for an approximation); TIMESTAMP_DIFF(…, MINUTE); COUNTIF. Snowflake: MEDIAN(minutes) or PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP, DATEDIFF('minute', …) (counts minute boundaries; exact here because times are whole minutes). Spark SQL: percentile(minutes, 0.5) interpolates like PERCENTILE_CONT; percentile_approx does not. MySQL 8: no median aggregate; rank rows with ROW_NUMBER() and COUNT(*) OVER and average the middle one or two.

Edge cases built into the data. Automated replies within a minute (sometimes the only host-side messages); guest follow-ups before the reply; a reply at exactly 1440 minutes and one at 1441; an inquiry with an automated reply, a guest follow-up and a real reply hours later; unanswered inquiries. Hard: support messages; inquiries created exactly at the window start (in) and end (out) and just before it; an in-window inquiry answered after the window; a host with only automated replies (median NULL, share 0); a host below the floor. Very Hard: co-hosts answering for the listing's host, including one who answers in minutes before the host does, and co-hosts' automated messages.

Common mistakes. Taking the first message after the inquiry from anyone; counting automated replies; filtering after MIN instead of before; an inner join that drops unanswered inquiries from the denominator; < 1440; the mean, or PERCENTILE_DISC, instead of the median; filtering replies by the window; ignoring co-hosts, or crediting the co-host as a separate host.

(1) Business-hours clocks pause outside a schedule in the host's time zone; computing them needs the host's time zone history and a working-time function; the meaning changes ("minutes of working time"), so name it differently. (2) Prefer the server receipt time for ordering and fairness; keep the client time for display; restate the inquiry's first reply when an earlier message arrives late, and recompute affected host aggregates. (3) Keep, per inquiry, created_at and first_reply_at (nullable), updated by message events; host aggregates are then recomputed from that small table, or maintained with mergeable sketches for medians. (4) Decide whether an inquiry that converts within N minutes is excluded from the denominator, encode that as a status on the inquiry, and document it next to the metric.

def orphan_gaps(min_stay, bookings, blocks):
    occupied = {lid: [] for lid in min_stay}
    for lid, start, end, status in bookings:
        if status == 'confirmed' and lid in occupied:
            occupied[lid].append((start, end))
    for lid, start, end in blocks:
        if lid in occupied:
            occupied[lid].append((start, end))
    out = {}
    for lid, spans in occupied.items():
        spans.sort()
        need = min_stay[lid]
        gaps = []
        run_end = None                        # end of the occupied run so far
        for start, end in spans:
            if run_end is not None and start > run_end and start - run_end < need:
                gaps.append((run_end, start))
            if run_end is None or end > run_end:
                run_end = end
        out[lid] = gaps
    return out

Explanation. Group the occupied intervals (confirmed bookings and blocks) by listing, sort each group by start, and sweep with the end of the current occupied run. An interval that starts after the run's end closes a gap (run_end, start); the gap is orphan when its length is positive and below the listing's minimum. The run's end only ever grows (max), which is what merges overlapping and touching intervals and keeps a short booking nested inside a long block from moving it backwards. Free nights before the first interval and after the last are never reported because a gap needs a run on both sides. Every listing in min_stay gets an entry, [] when it has nothing.

Complexity. O(n log n) for n bookings and blocks (the sorts), O(n) extra memory. The timing test (4 000 listings × 100 bookings, about 700 nights each, plus cancelled bookings and blocks at the higher levels) runs in about 0.7 s in CPython. A night-by-night scan that checks every booking of the listing for each night took about 0.5 s for 100 listings, so about 20 s for the full test; marking nights in a set is O(total nights) and passes here, but grows with calendar length rather than with bookings.

Dialect notes. In SQL this is the "gaps and islands" pattern: per listing, MAX(end) OVER (PARTITION BY listing ORDER BY start ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING) gives the run's end before each interval, and a gap exists where start > that. In Spark, the same window function, or groupBy(listing).applyInPandas with this sweep. In Java, sort an int[][] per listing with a comparator on start. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A gap one night shorter than the minimum (orphan) and exactly the minimum (not); back-to-back bookings; free nights before the first and after the last booking; a minimum stay of 1. Hard: cancelled bookings that would otherwise fill or bound a gap; unsorted input; a listing with no bookings. Very Hard: a block that bounds a gap; a block overlapping a booking and another block; a booking nested inside a long block; rows for a listing not in min_stay.

Common mistakes. <= instead of < against the minimum; reporting the edges of the calendar as gaps; using the previous interval's end rather than the running maximum (nested intervals); forgetting to filter cancelled bookings; leaving listings without gaps out of the result; a KeyError on unknown listings; per-night loops over every booking.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Use the minimum that applies to a stay starting on the gap's first night (check-in rules) or the strictest across it, and say which; the sweep is the same, the threshold becomes a lookup per gap. (2) A listing's calendar changes locally: re-sweep only that listing (its intervals are already sorted, so an insert is O(log n) with a sorted container, and only the neighbouring gaps change). (3) Partition by listing id hash; a listing never spans partitions, and per-listing work is tiny, so skew is not a concern unless one key holds many calendars (bucket by listing, not by host). (4) Compare orphan nights that were discounted with comparable ones that were not (a holdout of listings or dates), measuring sold nights and revenue, not just the discount uptake.

import math
from collections import defaultdict

CELL = 0.1                                    # degrees per grid cell
FIRST_COL, LAST_COL = math.floor(-180 / CELL), math.floor(180 / CELL) - 1


def _cell(x):
    return math.floor(x / CELL)


def search_map(listings, queries):
    grid = defaultdict(list)                  # (lat cell, lng cell) -> listings
    for item in listings:
        grid[(_cell(item[1]), _cell(item[2]))].append(item)
    out = []
    for south, west, north, east, page, size, max_price in queries:
        if south > north or page < 0 or size < 1:
            out.append((0, []))
            continue
        crosses = west > east
        if crosses:                           # [west, 180) and [-180, east]
            col_ranges = [(_cell(west), LAST_COL), (FIRST_COL, _cell(east))]
        else:
            col_ranges = [(_cell(west), min(_cell(east), LAST_COL))]
        r0, r1 = _cell(south), _cell(north)
        n_cells = (r1 - r0 + 1) * sum(c1 - c0 + 1 for c0, c1 in col_ranges)
        if n_cells <= len(grid):
            cells = [(r, c) for r in range(r0, r1 + 1) for c0, c1 in col_ranges for c in range(c0, c1 + 1)]
        else:                                 # a huge viewport: visit the occupied cells instead
            cells = [k for k in grid if r0 <= k[0] <= r1 and any(c0 <= k[1] <= c1 for c0, c1 in col_ranges)]
        hits = []
        for key in cells:
            for lid, lat, lng, price in grid.get(key, ()):
                if lat < south or lat > north:
                    continue
                if crosses:
                    if east < lng < west:
                        continue
                elif lng < west or lng > east:
                    continue
                if max_price is not None and price > max_price:
                    continue
                hits.append((price, lid))
        hits.sort()
        out.append((len(hits), [lid for _, lid in hits[page * size:(page + 1) * size]]))
    return out

Explanation. Listings are bucketed once into 0.1° cells. A viewport maps to a rectangle of cells, or to two column ranges when it crosses the antimeridian (west > east): from west's column to the last column before +180, and from the column of −180 to east's. Cells only narrow the candidates; every candidate is tested exactly against the viewport, so cell boundaries never decide membership and inclusive edges stay exact. Hits are sorted by (price, listing_id), which is the required order, then sliced for the 0-based page, with the total reported separately. A viewport that would touch more cells than are occupied (a whole-world view) iterates the occupied cells instead, so its cost is bounded by the index, not by the area. Invalid queries return the sentinel (0, []) before any work.

Complexity. Building the grid is O(N). A query costs O(cells touched + candidates + k log k) for k matches. The timing test (60 000 listings in 15 metros, 6 000 viewports of a few hundredths of a degree) runs in about 0.6 s in CPython. Scanning all listings per query took about 1.5 s per 300 queries, so about 30 s for the test.

Dialect notes. In PostgreSQL the same query is a GiST index on a point or PostGIS geometry with && against a box; an antimeridian-crossing box is split into two boxes combined with UNION ALL (or handled with geography types). In BigQuery, ST_INTERSECTSBOX(geo, west, south, east, north) accepts west > east for boxes crossing the antimeridian. In Java, a HashMap<Long, List<Listing>> keyed by a packed cell id. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A viewport crossing the antimeridian; listings exactly on all four edges; equal prices ordered by id, and a second page. Hard: invalid queries (south above north, negative page, page size 0) and a valid page size of 1; a page past the end with the total; a crossing viewport that includes −180 and a listing on its east edge but not one just east of it. Very Hard: max_price inclusive and None; a viewport one meridian wide; a whole-world viewport.

Common mistakes. west <= lng <= east for a crossing viewport (finds nothing); treating west > east as invalid; deciding membership by cell instead of by coordinates (edge listings lost or added); 1-based pages; returning the page size instead of the total; sorting by price only (unstable order across pages); rebuilding the index per query.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Adaptive structures (quadtrees, geohash or hierarchical cell prefixes, or a k-d tree) split dense areas finely and keep sparse ones coarse; uniform cells are simple and fine when the cell size matches typical viewports. (2) A small pan shares most cells with the previous viewport: cache per-cell candidate lists (sorted by price) and merge them; cache whole results by a quantized viewport. (3) A date-dependent total cannot be precomputed per listing for all date ranges; filter by availability first, then compute totals for the candidates, and page over that computed order. (4) Cursor paging (price > last_price OR (price = last_price AND id > last_id)) is stable under inserts and cheap for deep pages; page numbers shift items between pages when data changes.

Strong signals. Asks how a crossing viewport is represented before coding; tests the −180 / +180 seam; keeps exact filtering separate from bucketing. Red flags. Normalising longitudes by adding 360 to some listings and not others; distance from the viewport's centre in place of the rectangle.

from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right


def split_stays(calendars, queries, min_nights=None, capacity=None, no_single=False):
    rows = []
    for lid, cal in calendars.items():
        h = len(cal)
        fwd = [0] * (h + 1)              # fwd[t]: free nights starting at night t
        for t in range(h - 1, -1, -1):
            if cal[t] == ".":
                fwd[t] = fwd[t + 1] + 1
        back = [0] * (h + 1)             # back[t]: free nights ending just before night t
        for t in range(1, h + 1):
            if cal[t - 1] == ".":
                back[t] = back[t - 1] + 1
        m = min_nights.get(lid, 1) if min_nights else 1
        cap = capacity.get(lid) if capacity else None
        rows.append((fwd, back, max(1, m), cap))
    out = []
    for ci, co, guests in queries:
        d = co - ci
        if d < 2:
            out.append(0)
            continue
        firsts, seconds_lo, seconds_hi, both = [], [], [], 0
        for fwd, back, m, cap in rows:
            if cap is not None and cap < guests:
                continue
            p = min(fwd[ci], d)          # nights this listing can host from check-in
            s = min(back[co], d)         # nights it can host up to check-out
            if no_single and p == d and m <= d:
                continue                 # it could host the whole stay alone
            # k = nights in the first listing; the move happens after k nights
            lo1, hi1 = m, min(d - 1, p)
            lo2, hi2 = max(1, d - s), d - m
            ok1, ok2 = lo1 <= hi1, lo2 <= hi2
            if ok1:
                firsts.append((lo1, hi1))
            if ok2:
                seconds_lo.append(lo2)
                seconds_hi.append(hi2)
            if ok1 and ok2 and max(lo1, lo2) <= min(hi1, hi2):
                both += 1                # the same listing cannot be both halves
        seconds_lo.sort()
        seconds_hi.sort()
        ns = len(seconds_lo)
        total = 0
        for lo1, hi1 in firsts:
            disjoint = bisect_left(seconds_hi, lo1) + (ns - bisect_right(seconds_lo, hi1))
            total += ns - disjoint
        out.append(total - both)
    return out

Explanation. For one query of d nights, call k the number of nights in the first listing, so the move happens after k nights and 1 ≤ k ≤ d − 1. A listing can be the first half for exactly the k with k ≤ p (it is free for p nights in a row from check-in, capped at d) and k ≥ its minimum stay. It can be the second half for exactly the k with d − k ≤ s (free for s nights in a row up to check-out) and d − k ≥ its minimum stay. Both sets are intervals of k, so each listing becomes at most two intervals per query, and a pair works if and only if the first's "first" interval meets the second's "second" interval. Counting intersecting pairs is all pairs minus disjoint pairs: a pair is disjoint when the second interval ends before the first begins, or begins after it ends, and these two cases cannot both hold. With the second-role endpoints sorted, each first listing needs two binary searches. A listing whose own two intervals intersect would be counted as a pair with itself, so it is subtracted once. The free runs come from two linear passes per calendar, one backwards (fwd[t]) and one forwards (back[t]), so every query reads them in O(1) per listing. Capacity removes listings before anything else. With exclude_whole, a listing that is free for all d nights, has a minimum stay no longer than d and has room for the guests is dropped for that query only.

Complexity. Preparation is O(n · h). Each query is O(n log n) for the sorts and binary searches; with move-night counts below a few dozen, counting sort makes it O(n + d). The timing test (3 000 listings, 180 nights, 200 searches) runs in about 0.5 s in CPython. All pairs is 9 million pairs per query, and checking each pair's move nights night by night multiplies that again, so it takes hours. Recomputing the runs per query in O(n · d) and then counting with sorted intervals is fine.

Dialect notes. In Java or C++ the same structure uses int[] runs and Arrays.binarySearch or lower_bound / upper_bound; watch the inclusive and exclusive bounds, which are where most bugs are. In SQL, the per-listing runs are a gaps-and-islands query, and the pair count is a self-join on interval overlap (a.lo1 <= b.hi2 AND b.lo2 <= a.hi1 AND a.id <> b.id). That is correct but quadratic unless the engine can use a range join; counting disjoint pairs with window functions over sorted endpoints is the scalable form. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. A one-night stay; two halves that meet exactly on the move night; a gap night neither listing has; a listing that would pair with itself; two listings free for the whole stay (2 pairs, or 0 under exclude_whole); a stay that needs two moves; a stay from the first to the last night of the calendar; booked and blocked nights both unavailable; a query with no available listing. (Hard) A half of exactly the minimum stay and one night short; the minimum stay on the second listing; a pair whose latest move night breaks the second listing's minimum while an earlier one works; guests exactly at capacity and one more. (Very Hard) Whole-stay hosts excluded; a listing free for the whole stay but too small for the guests; one whose minimum stay is longer than the stay; whole-stay status decided per query.

Common mistakes. Counting unordered pairs; counting a pair once per move night; letting a listing pair with itself; not capping runs at the stay length, so a listing free for months gets an interval past d − 1; trying only the latest move night (fails with minimum stays); applying the minimum stay to one half only; treating 'x' as free; excluding whole-stay hosts globally instead of per query; quadratic pair loops.

Follow-up guidance. (1) For a fixed pair the price is linear in k, so the best move night is an end of the intersection. For top 20 overall, bucket listings by their interval ends; for each first listing, the cheapest compatible second listings at each possible k come from a precomputed "cheapest second listing whose interval contains k" list, then merge with a heap. Good candidates notice the structure, not just "sort by price". (2) Add a spatial filter: geohash or grid cells, pairs only within neighbouring cells; counting becomes per cell neighbourhood, and the interval trick still applies within it. (3) Keep runs per listing and night; a booked night changes fwd for the free run ending there and back for the run starting after it, so the update is bounded by the run length. Searches read the runs from the index. (4) Two moves add a middle listing that must be fully free on its segment; the count is a sum over middle listings and segments, and the number of combinations grows by another factor of n, so top-k with pruning becomes necessary.

Rubric anchors. 2: all pairs with night-by-night checks, or ordered pairs or self-pairs wrong; small tests only. 3: all tests pass with free runs and interval counting. 4: also explains why each role is an interval, derives the disjoint-pair formula cleanly, handles minimum stays on both sides first time, and gives a credible answer to the cheapest-pairs or update follow-up.

Strong signals. Asks whether (A, B) and (B, A) are different; states the interval of move nights per role before coding; tests the self-pair case. Red flags. Counts move nights instead of pairs; "it is only 3 000 listings" without estimating 9 million pairs times the searches per second.

def forward_occupancy(listings, bookings, start, end, window=30, blocked=None):
    lo, hi = start, end - 1 + window          # every night any window can touch
    span = hi - lo
    if span <= 0:
        return {lid: [] for lid in listings}
    book_diff = {lid: [0] * (span + 1) for lid in listings}
    for lid, ci, co, status in bookings:
        d = book_diff.get(lid)
        if d is None or status != "confirmed":
            continue
        a, b = max(ci, lo), min(co, hi)
        if a < b:
            d[a - lo] += 1
            d[b - lo] -= 1
    out = {}
    for lid in listings:
        d = book_diff[lid]
        blk = [0] * (span + 1)
        for a, b in (blocked or {}).get(lid, ()):
            a, b = max(a, lo), min(b, hi)
            if a < b:
                blk[a - lo] += 1
                blk[b - lo] -= 1
        pb = [0] * (span + 1)               # prefix: booked nights
        pu = [0] * (span + 1)               # prefix: unavailable (blocked, not booked) nights
        cb = ck = 0
        for i in range(span):
            cb += d[i]
            ck += blk[i]
            booked = cb > 0
            pb[i + 1] = pb[i] + booked
            pu[i + 1] = pu[i] + (ck > 0 and not booked)
        row = []
        for t in range(end - start):
            booked = pb[t + window] - pb[t]
            avail = window - (pu[t + window] - pu[t])
            row.append(round(booked / avail, 4) if avail else None)
        out[lid] = row
    return out

Explanation. Only nights from start to end − 2 + window can appear in any window, so every booking and block is clamped to that span. Each confirmed booking adds +1 at its check-in and −1 at its check-out on its listing's difference array. A running sum over the span gives, per night, how many bookings cover it, and the night is booked when that count is above zero, so overlapping bookings count once. Blocks use their own difference array, and a night is unavailable when it is blocked and not booked. Two prefix sums (booked nights, unavailable nights) turn each window into two subtractions: booked = pb[t + w] − pb[t], available = w − (pu[t + w] − pu[t]). A window with no available night is None, and a listing with no bookings still gets a full row of zeros. Bookings for unknown listings and cancelled bookings are skipped when the difference arrays are built.

Complexity. O(B + n · (D + w)) time and O(D + w) memory per listing, plus the output. The timing test (2 500 listings, 420 dates, a 150-night window, about 210 000 bookings) runs in about 1 s in CPython. Rescanning each window night by night, even with a set of booked nights per listing, is about 160 million checks and took about 16 s, well over the limit. A sliding window that adds the entering night and removes the leaving one is also linear and is accepted.

Dialect notes. In SQL, explode bookings into a nights table (generate_series(check_in, check_out - 1)), take MAX(booked) per listing and night to count overlaps once, left join to a listing × night spine, and use SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY listing ORDER BY night ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND w - 1 FOLLOWING). Snowflake, BigQuery and Spark SQL support the same frame; Spark needs care to avoid a full shuffle per window. In BigQuery, GENERATE_DATE_ARRAY and UNNEST explode the stays. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. The check-out night; a stay that began before the first date; one that runs past the last window; a listing with no bookings; a booking for an unknown listing; back-to-back stays; one date only; a 30-night window. (Hard) Blocked nights leaving the denominator; a window with every night blocked (None) followed by one with a free night (0); a booked night that is also blocked; overlapping blocks; a listing missing from blocked. (Very Hard) A cancelled booking; two confirmed bookings on the same nights; a cancelled and a confirmed booking on the same nights; overlaps, a cancellation and a block together.

Common mistakes. Counting the check-out night; dividing by window when blocks apply; reporting 0 instead of None when nothing is available, or raising ZeroDivisionError; summing booking lengths so overlapping bookings count twice; letting a cancelled booking's −1 cancel a confirmed booking's +1 (a sign of mixing statuses in one array); dropping listings with no bookings from the output; forgetting to clamp, so arrays sized by the furthest booking; O(n · D · w) loops.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Bookings need a created time and a cancelled time. The as-of curve is a sweep over observation dates: add a booking's nights when it is created and remove them when it is cancelled, with a Fenwick tree or segment tree over nights answering each window sum in O(log h). (2) Nights table plus window frame, as in the dialect notes; partition by market and listing, and avoid exploding stays of many months for every snapshot by keeping a nights table incrementally. (3) The ratio of sums is the market's real occupancy and weights big and small listings by their nights; the average of shares treats every listing equally and is what a "typical host" view wants. Pricing tools usually want the ratio of sums. (4) A booking for nights [a, b) changes the windows that start from a − w + 1 to b − 1, only for its listing; update those values or the prefix arrays from a on.

Rubric anchors. 2: nested loops or a set of nights per listing with rescans; the half-open rule or the None rule wrong. 3: all tests pass with difference arrays and prefix sums or a sliding window. 4: also explains the clamped span, why overlaps need "count above zero", and answers the as-of follow-up with a sweep over creation and cancellation times.

Strong signals. Asks whether bookings can overlap and whether blocked nights can be booked before coding; separates booked and unavailable counts cleanly. Red flags. Silently returns 0 for an all-blocked window; "the database never has overlapping bookings" with no check.

LONG_STAY_NIGHTS = 28      # this exercise's threshold for monthly payouts
PERIOD_NIGHTS = 30         # nights covered by each monthly payout


def _host_fee(gross, fee_bps):
    """The host service fee in cents: to the nearest cent, halves rounded up."""
    return (gross * fee_bps + 5000) // 10000                 # integers only


def host_payouts(bookings, fee_bps):
    lines = []                                    # (day, host, amount) per payout
    for b in bookings:
        nights = b["nights"]
        refunded = b.get("refund_nights", 0)
        paid = nights - refunded
        if paid <= 0:
            continue                              # fully refunded: nothing to pay
        cleaning = b["cleaning"]                  # kept unless every night is refunded
        if nights >= LONG_STAY_NIGHTS:
            for p in range(nights // PERIOD_NIGHTS + 1):
                first = p * PERIOD_NIGHTS
                last = min(first + PERIOD_NIGHTS, nights)
                paid_here = max(0, min(last, paid) - first)   # refunded nights are the last ones
                if paid_here == 0:
                    continue                      # no paid night, no payout
                gross = paid_here * b["rate"] + (cleaning if p == 0 else 0)
                lines.append((b["check_in"] + first + 1, b["host"],
                              gross - _host_fee(gross, fee_bps)))
        else:
            gross = paid * b["rate"] + cleaning
            lines.append((b["check_in"] + 1, b["host"], gross - _host_fee(gross, fee_bps)))
    transfers = {}
    for day, host, amount in lines:
        t = transfers.setdefault((day, host), [day, host, 0])
        t[2] += amount
    return sorted(transfers.values())

The planted bugs, their symptoms and their fixes.

  1. Transfers keyed by day only. transfers.setdefault(day, …) merges every host paid on the same day into the first host's transfer. Symptom: of two hosts whose guests checked in on the same day, one receives both payouts and the other none. Fix: key by (day, host).
  2. Half-to-even rounding. round(gross * fee_bps / 10000) uses Python's round, which rounds an exact half to the even cent, and divides in floating point first. Symptom: about half of the payouts whose fee ends in exactly half a cent are a cent off from the rule. Fix: (gross * fee_bps + 5000) // 10000 in integers (or Decimal with ROUND_HALF_UP on an exact quotient).
  3. Refunded nights taken from the start of a long stay. last - max(first, refunded) treats nights 0 … refunded − 1 as refunded. Symptom: after a guest leaves early, the first monthly payout is too small and a later one too large. Fix: the paid nights are 0 … paid − 1, so max(0, min(last, paid) - first).
  4. Cleaning fee dropped on a partial refund. cleaning = … if refunded == 0 else 0. Symptom: hosts lose the cleaning fee whenever any night is refunded. Fix: keep the cleaning fee unless every night is refunded, which the paid <= 0 check already handles.
  5. An empty period paid as a zero transfer. The loop creates nights // 30 + 1 periods, one too many when the stay is a multiple of 30 nights, and never skips a period with no paid night, which a refund at the end of a long stay also creates. Symptom: a $0.00 transfer a month after the last real payout. Fix: skip a period with no paid night (and optionally loop over ceil(nights / 30) periods).

Each bug has its own check: two hosts paid on the same day; a fee of exactly half a cent above an even number of cents; a 40-night stay with 5 nights refunded and no cleaning fee; a 6-night stay with a partial refund; a 60-night stay with no refund. Rates in those checks are chosen so that no other bug changes their result. The checks for a refund that empties a whole period and one that ends on a period boundary fail under both bugs 3 and 5; that is worth discussing once the candidate has fixed one of them and sees the check still failing.

Explanation. A payout run is a pure function from bookings to transfers. Each booking's paid nights are a prefix of its stay. For a monthly stay that prefix is cut into 30-night periods, each period's gross pays its own rounded fee, and transfers add payouts by host and day. Every money operation stays in integer cents.

Complexity. O(B + P log P) for B bookings and P payouts (the sort); a long stay contributes a handful of periods. The timing test is 100 000 bookings.

Dialect notes. In SQL, ROUND(numeric) in PostgreSQL rounds half away from zero, which equals half up for positive amounts; Snowflake's ROUND also rounds half away from zero by default, and BigQuery's ROUND does the same for NUMERIC (with ROUND(x, 0, 'ROUND_HALF_EVEN') available). Spark's round is half up and bround is half even. Rounding a FLOAT or DOUBLE in any engine can give a different cent from the exact value. Java's Math.round rounds half up for positives, and BigDecimal with RoundingMode.HALF_UP is the safe form. Not executed here.

Edge cases built into the tests. Two hosts paid on the same day; one host's two stays released on the same day (one transfer); a fee of exactly half a cent; a partial refund on a long stay; a partial refund on a short stay with a cleaning fee; exactly 60 nights; 27 and 28 nights; 31 nights; a fully refunded stay next to a paid one; a refund that empties a whole period; a refund that ends on a period boundary.

Common mistakes. Switching to Decimal but still building it from a float; computing the fee once per booking instead of per payout; deciding the monthly schedule from paid nights; keying transfers by booking id, which breaks "one transfer per host and day"; fixing the period count but not the empty-period skip, so refunds still create zero transfers; rewriting the calculator instead of making minimal fixes.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Record the refund as a negative adjustment against the booking and period, net it from the host's next transfer (or invoice it if none is due), and keep the original payout unchanged for audit. (2) Give every payout an idempotency key such as (booking id, period) and record sent keys in the same transaction as the transfer; a restarted run skips keys already sent. Keying by transfer alone is not enough, because a restart can regroup payouts. (3) A payout day is a calendar date, so state whose calendar it is. With the host's time zone, a run must process each zone's day when it ends there, and "the same day" for merging transfers is the host's day. (4) Per-transfer rounding changes a host's fee by at most half a cent per payout merged into the transfer, in either direction; show the distribution over a month of payouts, not a single example.

ABB-L2-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Source of truth. An availability store keyed by listing, with a row per listing and night (or per listing with a compact range map) and a version per listing. Night states: free, held (request pending, with an expiry), booked (booking id), host-blocked, import-blocked (feed id and event id). Bookings made here live in the bookings database; availability is written in the same transaction, or the booking's nights are protected by a constraint on the bookings table itself (for example an exclusion constraint on (listing_id, daterange(check_in, check_out)) for active bookings and holds).
  • Booking path. A booking request does a conditional write over its whole range: every night must be free (and not import-blocked) or the write fails. Instant-book confirms in the same transaction; a request-to-book creates a hold with an expiry. Expiry is a state transition with the same conditional check, not a cron job deleting rows.
  • Host app. Host blocks are conditional writes that refuse nights already booked or held, with a clear message.
  • Channel managers. An API that accepts snapshots of a date range or individual changes, each with a per-listing sequence number or the version it was based on. The write applies only if its sequence is newer than the last applied one; a retry with the same request id is a no-op. Snapshots replace only host-blocks and prices in their range, never bookings made here; a snapshot that says "free" over a booked night is recorded as a conflict.
  • Imported feeds. A fetcher schedules each feed by its refresh interval, with priority for listings in high demand and with conditional requests (ETag / If-Modified-Since) to keep fetches cheap. Each fetch is parsed and diffed against the previous fetch by event id: new ranges become import-blocks, removed ones are released. An import-block over a night booked here is a conflict, not an overwrite.
  • Change events. Every committed availability change emits an event (outbox pattern) keyed by listing with the new version. Search indexing and the exported feed consume it; the exported feed is regenerated per listing on change and served with caching headers, so other sites' polls see it quickly.
  • Conflict handling. A conflict record holds the listing, nights, both sides, the route that wrote each side and the detection time. Hosts are alerted at once; the workflow depends on which side is confirmed first (help the guest rebook, cancellation without penalty to the guest, and so on). Conflicts feed metrics by route and by connected tool.
  • Metrics. Double bookings per 10 000 bookings by route; import freshness distribution per feed; channel-manager write rejections by reason; time from a booking here to its appearance in the exported feed; search staleness (index version lag per listing).

Competing designs to accept. A single relational table with an exclusion constraint for bookings and holds, plus separate tables for host and import blocks; a per-listing actor or partition (all writes for a listing go through one ordered log) that serialises writes without database locks; an event-sourced availability log with a materialised calendar. Each is fine if overlapping confirmed stays are impossible and external writes are ordered and idempotent.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Hot listings with many concurrent requests (per-listing serialisation is fine because a listing's write rate is low; the danger is a global lock); long holds blocking nights; stale imports that the marketplace cannot fix by itself; snapshot writes that overwrite bookings; a search index that drops events; an exported feed cached for too long.

Incident guidance.

  • Imports fall an hour behind for a region: monitor feed freshness per provider and region; when lag exceeds a threshold, raise fetch priority for listings with upcoming demand, and, for listings whose only other channel is an import, consider asking hosts to confirm requests rather than instant-book until freshness recovers. Expect the conflict rate to rise and staff the support queue for it.
  • A channel manager sends all-free snapshots: snapshots never free a night booked here, so bookings are safe; the conflicts are logged. Detect the burst (free-night writes per tool far above normal), pause that tool's writes, and ask the provider; restore host blocks from the availability history, which is why it must be kept.
  • The search index misses changes after a restart: the index stores the last applied version per listing; a reconciler compares versions with the availability store and re-indexes listings that are behind. Bookings stay safe because the booking path never trusts the index.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The marketplace does not learn about the other booking until the next fetch or channel-manager update, so the exposure is the refresh interval; detection is at that fetch, followed by host notification and the conflict workflow. Good answers also shorten exposure by updating the exported feed immediately. (2) Version or sequence per listing: the late older snapshot is rejected, the retried batch is a no-op by request id. (3) Adaptive fetch frequency by demand and by how often the feed changes, conditional requests, and pushing hosts to connections that send changes instead of polled feeds. (4) Conflicts per route per 10 000 bookings, shown to hosts per connection with examples.

Rubric anchors. 2: a calendar table updated by every route with last write wins; no protection against overlapping bookings. 3: conditional booking writes or a constraint, separate import layer, idempotent channel-manager writes, change events to search. 4: also states the exposure window from polling and how to shrink it, models holds and conflicts explicitly, keeps availability history for recovery, and measures conflicts by route.

Strong signals. Separates what the marketplace can guarantee (its own bookings) from what it cannot (other sites' bookings); asks how channel managers identify their writes. Red flags. "Use a distributed lock" with no scope; trusting the search index or a cache at booking time.

ABB-L2-05.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Landing. Booking lifecycle events (created, altered, cancelled by guest or host, refund issued) land in an append-only table keyed by event id; duplicates are dropped on the event id. Each event keeps its event time and its arrival time, and the booking's currency and amounts in minor units.
  • Booking state history. A versioned table built from the events: one row per booking version with valid_from / valid_to (event time), check-in, check-out, guests, price, status, the cancellation policy recorded at booking time, and the version's source event. Late events are inserted in event-time order, and the versions after them are recomputed for that booking only.
  • Night-level fact. One row per booking and stay night with the night's amount, status (booked, cancelled, stayed), booking date, the version that created it and the version that ended it. An alteration from 7 nights to 4 ends three rows and keeps four (or ends and restarts them if the price changes). A cancellation marks the remaining future nights cancelled; a cancellation after check-in marks only the nights not stayed.
  • Refund fact. One row per refund event attached to booking and cancellation, with amount, currency, the rate used and the refund date. Partial and late refunds are simply more rows. An allocation of each refund to nights (pro rata, or by the policy's rule) lets the stay-date view carry refunded amounts per night.
  • Policy dimension. Policies are versioned with an id that never changes when a name does; bookings reference the id and the version in force at booking time.
  • Two views. By booking date: cohorts of bookings made in a period, with cancellations and refunds that happened at any later time, so last month's numbers keep moving until the cohort's last stay date has passed. By stay date: nights per stay date with their status and refunded amounts. Both read the same facts. A reconciliation report checks that, over all bookings made in a range whose stays have ended, total cancelled amounts and refunds agree in the two views.
  • Restatement. Reports for closed periods are published as versioned snapshots. When late events change a closed period, a new version is produced with a difference summary, and the published one is kept.
  • Currency. Store both the original currency and a reporting currency converted at a documented rule: the booking-date rate for booking value and the refund-date rate for refunds, with the conversion difference reported separately rather than hidden.

Competing designs to accept. Daily snapshots of booking state plus an event table (accept if the candidate shows what is lost between snapshots and why it does or does not matter); a fully event-sourced model where both views are computed from events on demand; a dbt-style layered model with incremental night facts. Any is fine if history is rebuildable and the two views reconcile.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. The night fact grows with bookings made far ahead (partition by stay month, cluster by listing); late events that force wide recomputation (recompute per booking, not per partition); renamed policies breaking joins; refunds without a cancellation (host-initiated goodwill refunds) that need their own reason; double-counting when an alteration is sent twice.

Incident guidance.

  • Refunds in 3 of the {{currencies}} currencies delayed four days: the by-booking-date refund amounts drop for recent cohorts, then recover. Show data completeness per currency and day on the report, hold publication of affected periods, and avoid alerting on a business drop that is really a pipeline delay.
  • Alterations sent twice with different event ids: the second copy must not move nights twice. Deduplicate on a business key (booking id, alteration content and a short time window) or make the alteration state-based (the new dates) rather than a delta, so applying it twice changes nothing.
  • A renamed policy: bookings reference a stable policy id, so the fact is unaffected; if the model joined on name, rebuild the affected rows, and add a test that every booking resolves to a policy.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The by-booking-date cohort of six weeks ago changes (its refunded amount), and the stay-date view changes for the cancelled nights' dates; closed periods change only through a recorded restatement. (2) Seven night rows; shortening ends three; cancellation marks the remaining four; the refund is attached to the cancellation and allocated to those nights. (3) State the rule; converting refunds at the refund date and bookings at the booking date makes money-based rates drift with exchange rates, so report rates in counts and in original currency too. (4) Training rows must use only the booking's state as of the prediction time: no later versions, no refund or cancellation fields, and features built from the versioned table with valid times.

Rubric anchors. 2: one booking table updated in place with a status column; no history; one view only. 3: event log, versioned booking state, night fact, refunds attached by event, both views defined. 4: also explicit metric grains and a reconciliation between views, restatement of closed periods, a currency rule, idempotency against duplicate alterations, and leakage protection for modelling.

Strong signals. Asks which date each team means before modelling; defines denominators for both views. Red flags. "Just overwrite the booking row"; a cancellation rate computed by stay date with a booking-date denominator.

ABB-L3-01.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design; score others on the criteria).

  • Identity and terms.
    • reservations (reservation_id, guest_id, host_id, created_at, current_version_id, status): identity only; the id never changes.
    • reservation_versions (version_id, reservation_id, version_no, listing_id, check_in, check_out, guests, quote_id, effective_at, created_by_alteration_id NULL): immutable. Version 1 is the booking; each accepted alteration adds one. "Terms as of T" = the version with the greatest effective_at ≤ T, where effective_at is the acceptance time (or the support action time).
  • Requests. alteration_requests (alteration_id, reservation_id, from_version_id, proposed_listing_id, proposed_check_in, proposed_check_out, proposed_guests, proposed_quote_id, proposed_by guest|host|support, proposer_id, reason, status proposed|accepted|declined|expired|withdrawn, responded_by NULL, responded_at NULL, expires_at). One open request per reservation (a partial unique index on reservation_id where status = 'proposed').
  • Quotes. price_quotes (quote_id, listing_id, check_in, check_out, guests, currency, nightly_total_minor, cleaning_fee_minor, service_fee_minor, tax_minor, total_minor, settings_version, quoted_at) plus line items. The difference is stored on the request at acceptance: delta_guest_minor (guest currency) and delta_host_minor (host currency), with the rates used.
  • Money. guest_charges (charge_id, reservation_id, alteration_id NULL, kind original|difference|refund, amount_minor, currency, fx_rate_id, status, idempotency_key) and payout_adjustments (adjustment_id, reservation_id, alteration_id, amount_minor, currency, status). One rule, stated: the original amount keeps the rate locked at booking; a difference uses the rate at acceptance.
  • Acceptance transaction. In one database transaction: check the request is still proposed and now() < expires_at; re-check the calendar for the new nights (the same availability lock or constraint that booking uses); insert the new version; mark the request accepted; insert pending charge/refund and payout adjustment rows (outbox). The payment provider is called after commit with the idempotency key; its result updates the charge row. If the charge ultimately fails, a follow-up state (payment_due) is visible to support, never a silent gap.
  • Facts.
    • fct_reservation_version (one row per version, with valid_from/valid_to): nights, guests, booking value; "booking value by stay date" uses the version in force at the report's as-of time.
    • fct_alteration (one row per request): proposer role, outcome, response time, nights delta, value delta in a reporting currency (stated conversion), month accepted.
    • fct_booking keeps one row per reservation (counted once at creation); alterations never create bookings.
  • Calendar. The calendar holds nights for the current version only; acceptance releases the old nights and holds the new ones in the same transaction.

Competing designs to accept. Event-sourced reservations (BookingCreated, AlterationProposed, AlterationAccepted…) with versions and facts as projections, if acceptance is checked against the current state. A type 2 dimension on reservations driven by acceptance time. Modelling an alteration as cancel-and-rebook is acceptable only if the candidate keeps the original id and fixes the booking and cancellation metrics explicitly; weak otherwise.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Overwriting the reservation row (lost agreement history, disputes unanswerable); cancel-and-rebook inflating bookings and cancellations; pending requests holding or not re-checking nights (double bookings); money edits instead of new records; adding currencies; payment outside the transaction without idempotency (double charges); expiry enforced only by a batch job.

Incident guidance.

  • Backfill counted alterations as new bookings: the booking fact was built from versions, not reservations. Rebuild bookings at reservation grain for the quarter, restate the dashboards with a note, and reverse the host performance flags that came from the inflated cancellation count; guard with a check that bookings per day = new reservation ids per day, and a test that an altered reservation contributes one booking. The size of the error is about {{alteration_share}} of reservations, which the check would have flagged.
  • Acceptance after expiry: expiry was a batch status, not a condition on acceptance. Contain by finding accepted requests whose responded_at > expires_at; offer the guest the choice to revert (a new version back to the old terms, with a refund of the difference); fix acceptance to check now() < expires_at in the same transaction; keep the job only for notifications. The window here is {{response_hours}} hours.
  • Timeout then double charge: the charge was not idempotent and its state was not recorded before calling the provider. Refund the duplicate, add an idempotency key per (alteration_id, kind), write the pending charge row in the acceptance transaction and reconcile charges against the provider's records daily; a reservation with a version that has no settled difference is listed for support.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Version 2 with 4 nights effective at acceptance; request accepted by the host; quote for the shorter stay; refund for nights not stayed (by this exercise's rules for refundable amounts) and a negative payout adjustment; nights already stayed are untouched. (2) The availability re-check inside the acceptance transaction fails; the request stays proposed or becomes declined with reason "dates unavailable"; nothing else is written. (3) As-of reporting: March loses the value, May gains it, labelled as a restatement after March closed — or March is frozen and the move appears as an adjustment in the month of acceptance; either, if stated. (4) Rate locked at booking for the original, rate at acceptance for the difference, both stored on the rows. (5) Requests, versions and charges are OLTP; facts are versions with valid_from/valid_to partitioned by month of effective_at; an as-of query is a range predicate.

Rubric anchors. 2: a reservation row updated in place, alterations as a log of text, or cancel-and-rebook without fixing metrics. 3: immutable versions, requests with lifecycle and actors, quotes and a stored difference, money as linked records, calendar re-check. 4: also atomic acceptance with an outbox and idempotent payments, expiry enforced at acceptance, a stated currency rule, as-of facts that keep booking counts stable, and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Asks what both parties saw when they agreed; distinguishes request time from acceptance time. Red flags. Deleting the old terms; editing the original payment amount; booking counts that move with alterations.

ABB-L3-02.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Experience and versions. experiences (experience_id, primary_host_id, city_id, time_zone, created_at, status); experience_versions (experience_id, version_no, title, description, duration_min, meeting_point, inclusions, price_per_guest_minor, private_group_price_minor, currency, max_group, min_guests, valid_from). Material fields (time, duration, meeting point, price) change only through a new version; existing bookings keep theirs.
  • Co-hosts. experience_hosts (experience_id, host_id, role primary|cohost, valid_from, valid_to).
  • Schedules and instances. schedules (schedule_id, experience_id, rule weekly-day-and-local-time, valid_from_date, valid_to_date); instances (instance_id, experience_id, schedule_id NULL, local_date, local_start_time, time_zone, starts_at_utc derived, capacity, mode open|shared|private, status scheduled|cancelled|completed, cancel_reason NULL, cancelled_by NULL). Instances are materialised for a rolling horizon (e.g. 90 days); a changed pattern regenerates only instances with no bookings and flags booked ones for the host to keep or cancel with notice.
  • Bookings. bookings (booking_id, instance_id, booker_id, guest_count, kind shared|private, version_no, price_minor, currency, status, booked_at, cancelled_at NULL, cancelled_by NULL, reason NULL), attendees (booking_id, seq, name NULL).
  • Capacity invariant. instances.seats_taken updated in the same transaction as the booking with UPDATE instances SET seats_taken = seats_taken + :n WHERE instance_id = :id AND mode <> 'private' AND seats_taken + :n <= capacity (zero rows updated = rejected). A private booking requires seats_taken = 0 and sets mode = 'private'; a shared booking sets mode = 'shared' when it is the first. A nightly reconciliation compares seats_taken with Σ guest_count of active bookings.
  • Time. Local date and time plus an IANA time zone are the truth; UTC is derived per instance and recomputed if the zone rules change.
  • Facts. fct_instance (one row per instance: capacity, seats sold, mode, status, minimum met), fct_booking (price, currency, reporting conversion), fct_cancellation (actor guest|host|minimum_not_met|support, reason). Fill rate = seats sold ÷ capacity over completed shared instances; private instances reported separately (count and group size), never in the seat-based rate.

Competing designs to accept. Row lock (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) on the instance instead of a conditional update. Instances generated on demand from rules and persisted at first booking (lazy), if reporting knows which instances existed. Separate tables for private bookings. A seat-level table (one row per seat) for small groups.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. Capacity computed from the current version (retroactive over-capacity); UTC-only start times; check-then-insert races; private and shared bookings on one instance; regenerating a pattern deletes booked instances; fill rate mixing private and shared; revenue summed across currencies.

Incident guidance.

  • Capacity lowered, bookings auto-cancelled: capacity belonged to the instance at the time it was created and booked, not to the current version. Restore the cancelled bookings (notify and apologise), make capacity an instance field changed only for unbooked instances, and add a rule that no automated job cancels guests. Lowering below {{max_group}} affects only new instances.
  • Instances an hour early after a clock change: the pattern was expanded with a fixed UTC offset. Recompute starts_at_utc from local time and the zone for affected instances, notify booked guests, and add a test that expands a weekly pattern across a daylight-saving transition.
  • Private bookings counted in fill rate: report private instances separately; recompute fill rate over shared instances; at about {{private_share}} private instances the distortion is large for some hosts, so restate their history and tell them.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Both try the conditional update; one wins. If the shared booking wins, the private request fails (seats_taken > 0); if the private wins, the shared fails (mode private). Only the winner's booking row exists. (2) Unbooked Saturday instances are cancelled or deleted (never existed for guests); booked ones remain until the host cancels with notice, recorded as host cancellations with reason "schedule change". (3) The version at booking holds the price; revenue uses the booking's price and currency. (4) Seats sold ÷ capacity for completed shared instances; cancelled instances counted separately; final after the instance date. (5) Materialise a rolling horizon; beyond it compute from rules; at {{experiences}} experiences this keeps instance rows bounded.

Rubric anchors. 2: one experiences table with a schedule text field and bookings counted without a transactional check. 3: versions, instances, bookings with version and price, a transactional capacity invariant, local time with a zone. 4: also private/shared exclusivity, pattern changes that respect booked instances, metric definitions that separate private bookings, and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. States the capacity invariant as SQL; asks how a pattern change treats booked instances. Red flags. Storing only UTC; SELECT COUNT(*) then INSERT without a lock; editing the price of existing bookings.

ABB-L3-03.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Reviews. reviews (review_id, reservation_id, author_role guest|host, author_id, subject_id, eligible_at (checkout), window_closes_at (end of day checkout + {{review_window_days}} days in the listing's zone, as an instant), submitted_at NULL, published_at NULL, status eligible|draft|submitted|published|removed, overall_rating NULL, public_text NULL); unique (reservation_id, author_role).
  • Publication rule. published_at = LEAST(window_closes_at, GREATEST(guest.submitted_at, host.submitted_at)) when both are submitted, else window_closes_at for the one that exists. A small job writes published_at, but every read path also filters published_at <= now() computed from the timestamps (view or row-level policy), so a late job delays nothing and an early job cannot leak.
  • Sub-ratings. review_subratings (review_id, category, score) and review_categories_asked (review_id, category); averages per category use only reviews that were asked that category.
  • Private feedback. private_feedback (review_id, text) in a separate table with access limited to the subject host's own views; excluded from the warehouse's analyst tables or kept in a restricted schema.
  • Responses. review_responses (response_id, review_id, version, text, posted_at).
  • Reports and removals. review_reports (report_id, review_id, reporter, reason, at), review_moderation (review_id, decision removed|kept|restored, policy_reason, decided_at, appeal_of NULL). Removal sets status removed; text is retained for audit with restricted access.
  • Listing rating. A dated series fct_listing_rating_daily (listing_id, date, published_count, rating_sum, per-category sums and counts) built from publication and removal events; the shown rating on date D = sum ÷ count of reviews published ≤ D and not removed ≤ D, shown only when count ≥ {{min_reviews_shown}}. Restatement rule stated: past dates either reflect what was shown (removal not back-dated) or are restated (removal back-dated) — pick one and label it.
  • Facts. fct_review (one row per review: role, eligible, submitted, published, removed, days to submit), review rate by role = submitted ÷ eligible per checkout cohort, final after the window.

Competing designs to accept. A single table with nullable guest and host halves per reservation (works if the visibility rule is still timestamp-derived). An event log of review state changes with projections. A materialised visible_reviews table refreshed frequently, if leaks are impossible by construction (only published rows copied).

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A visibility boolean set by a job (late or early publication); window computed in UTC; sub-ratings as columns; averages kept as running sums that cannot subtract; private feedback in analyst-visible tables; deletes on removal; small-count averages leaking hidden information.

Incident guidance.

  • Early publication from UTC window close: hold publication for affected reviews not yet seen (if any), apologise to affected parties, fix window_closes_at to use the listing's zone, and add a test across zones and a check that no review is published before both submitted or window_closes_at. The window here is {{review_window_days}} days.
  • Stale averages after removals: the cached sum never decreased. Recompute ratings from published, non-removed reviews; make removal an event that updates the series; add a daily reconciliation of cached ratings against a recomputation. Removals run at about {{removal_share}} of reviews, so drift grows steadily without it.
  • Hidden rating inferable from a dashboard: the dashboard read submitted rather than published reviews. Withdraw it, rebuild it from the published view only, apply the same {{min_reviews_shown}} threshold to every host-facing aggregate, and add a test that unpublished reviews never reach host-facing tables.

Follow-up guidance. (1) The host's review publishes at window_closes_at; the read-path predicate makes it visible even if the job is late. (2) Averages per category over reviews that were asked; report the count with each average. (3) Choose and state: the shown-history is kept (removal from its date) or restated; host performance uses the same rule. (4) Analysts get the published view only; private feedback in a restricted schema; a CI test greps for joins to it. (5) Definition with the threshold, published ≤ D, removed > D or never.

Rubric anchors. 2: a boolean visibility flag, sub-rating columns, a running average. 3: timestamps that derive publication, long-form sub-ratings, private feedback isolated, removals as states, a derived rating. 4: also a read-path guarantee against leaks, zone-correct windows, a dated rating series with a restatement rule and threshold, and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Treats "hidden" as a security property of every read path, not a UI rule. Red flags. Deleting removed reviews; private feedback in general analyst tables; averages without counts.

ABB-L3-04.html:
Reference architecture (one defensible design).

  • Settings as rules (append-only, bitemporal). price_rules (rule_id, listing_id, kind base|weekend|custom_date|cleaning_fee|los_discount|currency, nights_from DATE NULL, nights_to DATE NULL, min_nights NULL, amount_minor NULL, percent NULL, currency, recorded_at, superseded_at NULL, changed_by). recorded_at/superseded_at is system time (when the setting was in force); nights_from/nights_to (half-open) is which nights it applies to. A change supersedes the old rule and inserts a new one; nothing is updated except superseded_at.
  • Price function. For night N as of time T: rules in force at T (recorded_at ≤ T < superseded_at), precedence custom_date ⟶ weekend (Friday or Saturday by the night's local date) ⟶ base. Stay total = Σ nightly prices × (1 − largest applicable length-of-stay percent) + cleaning fee. Implemented once in the pricing service and replayed for audits.
  • Settings version. A per-listing monotonically increasing settings_version bumped on every change; quotes and calendar rows carry it.
  • Nightly calendar (serving). listing_night_price (listing_id, night, price_minor, currency, settings_version, computed_at) for the next 365 nights, recomputed for the affected nights on each change (event-driven), with a sweeper that compares the stored version with the listing's current version.
  • Quotes. quotes (quote_id, listing_id, check_in, check_out, guests, settings_version, nightly_breakdown, discount_kind, discount_minor, cleaning_fee_minor, fees_minor, taxes_minor, total_minor, currency, quoted_at, expires_at, surface search|listing|checkout). Checkout quotes kept in full forever (they are evidence for bookings); search quotes sampled or kept in full for a short period (e.g. 30 days) and aggregated after. bookings.quote_id references the checkout quote.
  • Facts. fct_quote_daily (market, stay date, surface, avg nightly price, count), fct_booking_price (discount kind, discount amount), fct_price_mismatch (search quote vs checkout quote for the same session: total difference and reason — settings changed, quote expired, guests or dates changed).

Competing designs to accept. SCD type 2 per setting type in separate tables. Snapshotting the full settings document per change (JSON) with a version id, if the price function reads it. A calendar-only design where hosts edit nightly prices directly, if each nightly price change is append-only and quotes carry the version.

Bottlenecks and failure modes. A price column overwritten (history lost); confusing system time with valid nights; weekend computed from UTC; discount stacking; the serving calendar drifting from settings with no version to detect it; storing every search quote forever at {{quotes_per_day}} a day; currency changes that rewrite old amounts.

Incident guidance.

  • Weekly and monthly discounts stacked: the precedence rule lived in code without a test. Contain by fixing the function and re-quoting open quotes; for bookings made in the window, decide with policy who absorbs the difference (in most designs the platform tops up host payouts rather than charging guests more); add a property test that at most one length-of-stay discount applies and a monitor on the share of quotes with two discounts. With discounts like {{weekly_discount}}, the affected bookings are easy to find from quotes' discount_kind.
  • Calendar an hour behind: quotes carry settings_version, so the mismatch is measurable: compare each quote's version with the version in force at quoted_at. Scale the recompute workers for bursts above the usual {{setting_changes}} a day, alert on calendar version lag, and at checkout always recompute from rules, never from the calendar.
  • Weekend applied to the wrong nights east of UTC: the weekday came from a UTC timestamp. Compute it from the night's date in the listing's zone; re-quote open quotes; identify bookings made in the window from their stored breakdown and correct per policy; add tests with listings far east and west of UTC.

Follow-up guidance. (1) Seven nights Thu→Thu: Friday and Saturday at the weekend price unless one is custom; the custom night at its price; {{weekly_discount}} off the nightly total; then the cleaning fee. Reads: rules in force at quote time for that listing. (2) Search at 13:59 used version v; booking at 14:05 re-quoted under v+1; both quotes stored; the mismatch fact records "settings changed". (3) Checkout quotes forever; search quotes in full for a short period, then aggregates. (4) Average offered price for 31 December by quote date: from fct_quote_daily (or by replaying rules at past times on a sample). (5) A currency change is a dated rule; custom prices are re-expressed or cleared by stated policy; open quotes expire; history stays in the old currency.

Rubric anchors. 2: a listing table with price columns updated in place. 3: effective-dated append-only rules, a precedence order, quotes stored with a version and referenced by bookings. 4: also both times kept apart (bitemporal), a materialised calendar reconciled by version, a quote retention plan, local-date weekend logic, and correct incident handling.

Strong signals. Separates "when the setting was in force" from "which nights it applies to" unprompted; treats quotes as evidence. Red flags. Recomputing a past booking's price from current settings; summing currencies; no version on quotes.

ABB-L3-05.html:
Reference solution (PostgreSQL)

WITH latest_accepted AS (                     -- per reservation, the accepted alteration resolved last
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (reservation_id) reservation_id, new_check_in, new_check_out
  FROM reservation_alterations
  WHERE status = 'accepted'
  ORDER BY reservation_id, resolved_at DESC
), stays AS (
  SELECT r.reservation_id, r.listing_id,
         COALESCE(a.new_check_in,  r.check_in)  AS check_in,
         COALESCE(a.new_check_out, r.check_out) AS check_out
  FROM reservations r
  LEFT JOIN latest_accepted a ON a.reservation_id = r.reservation_id
  WHERE r.status = 'confirmed'
), nights AS (                                -- half-open: check_in <= night < check_out
  SELECT s.listing_id, s.reservation_id, s.check_in + k AS night
  FROM stays s
  CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series(0, s.check_out - s.check_in - 1) AS k
), overbooked AS (
  SELECT n.listing_id, n.night, COUNT(*) - l.units AS excess
  FROM nights n
  JOIN listings l ON l.listing_id = n.listing_id
  GROUP BY n.listing_id, n.night, l.units
  HAVING COUNT(*) > l.units
), involved AS (
  SELECT n.listing_id, COUNT(DISTINCT n.reservation_id) AS reservations_involved
  FROM nights n
  JOIN overbooked o ON o.listing_id = n.listing_id AND o.night = n.night
  GROUP BY n.listing_id
)
SELECT l.listing_id,
       l.city,
       COUNT(*)      AS overbooked_nights,
       SUM(o.excess) AS excess_stay_nights,
       i.reservations_involved,
       MIN(o.night)  AS first_night
FROM overbooked o
JOIN listings l ON l.listing_id = o.listing_id
JOIN involved i ON i.listing_id = o.listing_id
GROUP BY l.listing_id, l.city, i.reservations_involved
ORDER BY excess_stay_nights DESC, l.listing_id;

Explanation. The effective stay comes first: one accepted alteration per reservation (the one resolved last) laid over the originally booked dates with COALESCE, and only for confirmed reservations. Each stay is expanded into its nights with the half-open rule (check_in + 0 … check_out − check_in − 1), so a check-out date is never a night. Counting stays per (listing, night) and keeping the counts above the listing's units gives the overbooked nights and their excess; the reservations involved are found by joining the nights back to those overbooked nights, with COUNT(DISTINCT …) because a reservation usually covers several of them.

Complexity. Linear in the number of stay-nights (Σ nights per counted reservation) plus one hash aggregate per step; the alteration pick is a sort or hash over accepted alterations.
